analysis.one_liner: Phases out feeding medically important antibiotics to farm animals for growth promotion, to slow antibiotic-resistant infections.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by a bipartisan group of four senators and more than 300 health, consumer, and farm organizations, never received a committee vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require drug makers to prove that antibiotics routinely added to livestock feed and water — not to treat sick animals, but to speed growth and compensate for crowded conditions — do not endanger human health by breeding drug-resistant bacteria. Any use it couldn't prove safe would be phased out within two years. It pairs the phase-out with federal payments to help farmers, prioritizing small family farms, transition away from routine antibiotic use, funds university research on how to raise animals without it, and requires drug makers to report and publish annual antibiotic sales data.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who depend on antibiotics working when they get sick. Routine feeding of antibiotics to livestock accelerates the spread of bacteria that resist those drugs, making common infections like Salmonella and E. coli harder and more expensive to treat. Small family farms also benefit: they get priority for federal payments to cover the cost of changing practices, and university extension programs would teach proven methods for raising animals without routine antibiotics.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that any antibiotic critical to human medicine be proven safe from breeding resistance before it can be routinely fed to farm animals, and withdraws approval for nontherapeutic uses within two years unless safety is demonstrated [S2] [S3].

Targets the practice identified in the bill's findings as the source of an estimated 70% of U.S. antibiotic use — feeding antibiotics to farm animals for growth promotion and to compensate for crowded, unsanitary conditions [S3].

Authorizes payments to livestock and poultry producers who substantially reduce routine antibiotic use, with priority for family-owned and small farms, plus grants to colleges to research and demonstrate how to raise animals without them [S2] [S3].

Requires manufacturers to report annual antibiotic sales by animal type and purpose, and to publish the data, closing a gap a GAO report said blocks agencies from assessing human health risks [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of medicated animal feeds and antibiotics lose their largest market: routine, non-prescription use in livestock. Large industrial livestock producers would face costs of changing how they raise animals, though federal payments would defray some of the transition. The bill's own findings cite National Academy of Sciences estimates that eliminating feed additives would cost consumers less than $5 to $10 per year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Feed-additive makers and large livestock producers

drawbacks.text: Livestock producers argued routine antibiotics control disease in crowded herds and flocks; the bill acknowledges this by allowing therapeutic and documented disease-control uses, but producers would still face real transition costs and some risk to productivity [S3].

Withdrawal of existing approvals within two years is aggressive: most of these drugs were approved decades before FDA evaluated resistance, and producers would have limited time to prove safety or restructure operations [S3].

Drug and feed makers bear compliance costs of proving safety and reporting sales annually, costs that could be passed into feed and meat prices, though the bill's findings put the consumer cost at under $5-$10 a year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and durable: preserving the effectiveness of antibiotics used in human medicine, a threat the bill's findings say already costs society $4-5 billion a year. The costs fall on a concentrated set of drug and feed makers and industrial producers, with federal transition payments to soften the burden on small farms. The main honest objection is the two-year timeline, which is fast for restructuring livestock operations — but the EU's similar ban, cited in the bill, showed no significant impact on animal health, food safety, or meat prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on February 12, 2007, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Snowe (R-ME), Reed (D-RI), and Brown (D-OH) [S3].

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; the action history shows no markup, no vote, and no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5] [S1].

The bill's findings document support from more than 300 organizations, including the American Medical Association and the American Public Health Association, and note that the European Union banned the practice in 1999 with no significant impact on animal health or meat prices [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of antibiotics and medicated animal feeds, and large livestock operations that rely on routine antibiotic use to keep animals growing quickly in crowded conditions, were better off because the bill died without ever reaching a vote. The public health cost — continued routine use of medically important antibiotics in livestock — fell on everyone else.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Feed-additive makers and large livestock producers

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, citing federal task force and National Academy of Sciences findings that antibiotic resistance is a growing public health threat and that agriculture is the largest source of the overuse.

for.name: Sens. Olympia Snowe, Jack Reed, and Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making it bipartisan from day one.

for.name: More than 300 health, consumer, agricultural, and environmental organizations
for.role: Supporting coalition, including the American Medical Association and American Public Health Association
for.what_they_did: Backed enactment, as catalogued in the bill's own findings section.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired in the 110th Congress by Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it received no action beyond referral for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Antibiotic and medicated feed manufacturers and large livestock producers
against.role: Industries whose routine-use market the bill would phase out
against.what_they_did: The industries affected by the bill had every incentive to keep it from advancing; no organized support for the bill from these sectors appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction — a Democrat sponsoring with one Republican and two Democratic cosponsors — and was never opposed on any recorded vote, because it never got one.

industries.industry: Antibiotic and medicated animal feed manufacturers
industries.note: The bill phases out their largest, non-prescription market: routine antibiotics in livestock feed and water, which the bill's findings say account for roughly 70% of U.S. antibiotic use. It also imposes annual sales reporting and puts the burden on them to prove their products don't breed resistance.

industries.industry: Large industrial livestock and poultry producers
industries.note: Producers would lose growth promotion and the cheap substitute for cleaner, less crowded conditions, and would face transition costs the bill partially offsets with federal payments. Their interest in keeping routine antibiotics runs against the public's interest in antibiotics that still work.

They get priority for federal payments to defray the cost of reducing antibiotic use, and extension programs would teach alternatives — support designed so the phase-out doesn't fall hardest on small operations.
